items.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
items.author: QueensGambit
items.content:
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:

  1. First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation.
  2. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID.
  3. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.
All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.

What is the right code for this?

If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:
  1. Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone.
  2. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.
In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack.
AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.
Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.

Your new job is to architect

AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:
  1. Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app.
  2. Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.
That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.
If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.

items.title: Vibecoding an inference chip
items.author: ankitvgupta
items.content:
One of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely new domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms. Lately, that has meant hacking on hardware, now that writing low-level software is much easier. So, in this blog post, I’m going to try to recount the experience of vibe coding an FPGA, going through a series of “oh shit” moments several times, and giving myself a new appreciation for what’s possible if you have a large token budget (thanks YC) and interesting problems to point the models at.

I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work. I’ll admit I was relatively naive about them. I’d never really experimented with them in my startup or in college, so I knew little about them before. The basic idea I was familiar with: you can program a circuit into a reprogrammable chip. So rather than having a general purpose computing architecture (like a CPU) you can have a reprogrammable one, i.e. the configuration loaded onto the chip determines how its logic and routing are connected, and that (in theory) enables performance advantages. I also know that it took a mountain of C++ to write and involved manually analyzing waveforms for simulation and verification. I had never done this before though and it seemed cumbersome.

That’s about what I knew going into this.

Naturally, my ML brain thought “could we use these for AI inference”. I’m not the first to think this — there are a few repos attempting to port ML models to FPGAs on Github. But I hadn’t actually seen a writeup on whether coding agents are good at writing the low level C++ and Verilog code to program them and verifying the outputs so that they actually run accurately. (Spoiler alert, they are incredible at programming them.)

So I decided I needed to get my hands on one. AWS has F2 instances with FPGA hardware, and that seemed easier than going and buying physical hardware, so I asked Codex to spin up a reservation and got cooking. It had a relatively limited memory of 16 GB of FPGA HBM. Around the same time, I was working with the DeepGrove founders who were discussing their new ternary weight architecture that is well suited for memory limited cases. It’s SOTA on Mac hardware with actual agentic tool calling, so I figured why not, let’s see if I can get this working on an FPGA and fast enough to be useful.

What followed was a cloud agent running in Conductor for several days with me mostly just encouraging it periodically while it both (1) got a model fully running and (2) increased its speed by 33× from the first full-model bit-exact baseline to get it to a real-time relevant speed. It was one of the most mind blowing autoresearch loops I’ve run, ultimately writing roughly 3M lines across the experiment history and parsing 30M lines of output files, burning only $10,000 in Claude and OpenAI tokens to run hundreds of experiments. Most of the code is C++ and some Verilog. It’s been probably a decade since the last time I wrote any serious amount of C++ and I’ve never written Verilog. I honestly don’t know the first thing about Verilog. Most of my prompts were not particularly clever: they consisted mostly of me saying things like “you’re a superintelligent model, time to be more creative” and “let’s go for 2x faster, you got this”. Sometimes I brought some ML knowhow like “hey it’s time to consider speculative decoding” or “why is that running on CPU, you should port it”. But for the most part, it was just vibes and I’m pretty sure that with enough time the model would have figured out those things. Also, it seemed that both Astra and Opus (new Fable wasn’t out yet) were pretty capable at this and I could use them interchangeably. I’m sure someone has a good benchmark for which is smarter but both passed my smart-enough threshold.

From “it works” to 213 tokens per second

The chart follows the measured optimization sequence: , or the baseline.

How much did the human advice help?

At one point, around when it got to 10 TPS, I messaged the DeepGrove founders about this, and they replied surprised that it was working so easily, saying they had tried this a few months back and the models were not quite good enough to be particularly effective. They sent me a prompt that summarizes some of their lessons and I copy-pasted it into my session to see if it’d matter. It was essentially the most significant piece of actual guidance I added to this session. The prompt is reproduced below.

The coding agent diligently considered these asks, but it didn’t seem to make all that much of a difference qualitatively. Indeed, when I asked it later to read all of the logs and determine which of these instructions it actually used, it said:

In other words, for most of the actual design ideas it is unclear but there is good reason to believe the model would have figured them out, especially because it came up with them many cycles later after several compaction cycles. But the process advice was useful immediately for getting to hardware results sooner and increasing iteration speed. In other words, the humans are still useful at defining how to iterate fast and what correctness looks like, and the agents are great to manage the exploration.

Here are the changes the autoresearch loop found. Interestingly, it’s mostly a series of modest improvements that compound 1.5x ish every time, rather than one or two giant ones.

It’s difficult to do a 1:1 comparison across these configurations. I didn’t run the same autoresearch loop on every alternative, and I assume there is more performance to extract if I did. The point is to show how slow the FPGA was in its first implementation, and how far the optimization loop took it.

The measurements below are from November 15 on AWS, replaying the same 8-chat × 3-turn benchmark. Prices are the on-demand rates recorded with that experiment. “Exact turns” counts outputs that matched the pinned CPU reference. The GPU implementations are included for context but did not satisfy the same bit-exact criterion but are pretty close in practice.

What happens as the context grows?

This is one generation starting with a 16-token prompt and continuing until the 8,192-token context is full: . The five middle columns show decode speed in at the indicated context length for several generations of iteration. The last column is wall-clock time for the whole run/

* For r8 and r9, the first two columns come from separate, shorter runs generating 2,032 tokens. The other columns come from the full-context run.

r9 improves short-context speed, while the complete long-context run is roughly tied with r8.

What the model actually says

These examples come from the final r9 image.

Arithmetic, with the steps

System prompt: “You are a helpful assistant. Think briefly before you answer, then reply clearly and concisely.”

This was a fun project. I’m not sure I’m ever going to use this specific chip architecture in this specific way, and I’m certainly not claiming that an 8,192-token-context model running on an FPGA is the way I’d recommend anyone use something like this in production. But it’s pretty epic that this . Capability like this completely shifts the overton window for what a committed team of engineers can work on. It should mean that entirely new types of ideas (scientific discoveries, products, startups) are possible if you can point the models in the right direction. I’m excited to see what everyone builds.

items.title: Top 13 Microservices Interview Questions Answered
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Last year, I met a young software engineer who walked into an interview, confident he knew the fundamentals.

But he struggled to answer some simple questions about microservices.

His story is why I wrote this letter.

  • Design your system architecture in Miro

  • Document API, database & caching decisions

  • Connect Claude Code through Miro’s MCP server

  • Retrieve the architecture context from the Miro board

  • Generate an implementation plan based on that context

  • Bring the plan back to Miro for team review

I tried this workflow with a URL shortener architecture & it saved me hours of work.

It lets your coding agent work with existing architecture decisions, so you can spend less time repeating context and more time building.

(Thanks to Miro for partnering on this newsletter.)

Here are the top 13 must-know interview questions with answers:

“What problems do microservices solve & what new problems do they create?”

Microservices split one application into small services, each running in its own process and deployed independently.

An online shop might run separate services for catalog, cart, payments, and shipping. Each has its own code, data, and release schedule. Services talk over the network through application programming interfaces ().

A small group of engineers owns each service from design to production.

  • They solve coordination problems. Each group ships its own service without waiting for a shared release.

  • Also they let you scale each service independently. A busy search service gets more instances while the rest stay small.

  • Yet they create network problems. Every call can be slow, fail, or arrive twice.

  • Plus, they create data problems. No single database transaction spans services, so you need sagas or eventual consistency.

  • And they need tooling before the first service goes live: service discovery, tracing, and automated deployment.

“How do you decide where to draw the line between two services?”

Split along business capabilities, such as payments/shipping, not technical layers.

Each service should own its data and change for one business reason. If two services always deploy “together or call each other” on every request, they belong in one service.

Listing only the benefits.

This question tests whether you know the costs. “Microservices are more scalable” with no mention of network failures or split data sounds like you’ve only read about them.

Strong candidates also say when not to use them, such as a small product with a handful of engineers.

“What’s the difference between an API gateway & a load balancer?”

An API gateway is a single entry point that receives every client request and routes it to the right service.

The gateway handles the work every request needs. It checks the token, applies rate limits, and validates the request. Then it finds the target service and forwards the call.

It also merges several service responses into one reply for the client.

  • A load balancer spreads traffic across copies of one service.

  • While a gateway reads paths, headers, and tokens, then decides which service gets the request.

  • They work together. A load balancer sits in front of several gateway instances.

“Your gateway is becoming a bottleneck. What do you do?”

Keep the gateway stateless and run more instances behind the load balancer.

Cache token checks. Move heavy work like response merging into “backend for frontend”. If it’s still too much, split the gateway by domain.

Putting business rules in the gateway, such as discount logic.

The gateway then changes with every feature and needs every group’s sign-off, which recreates the enterprise service bus problem.

“Compare client-side and server-side service discovery.”

Service discovery is how a caller finds a healthy instance of the service it wants to reach.

In discovery, the caller queries the registry itself. It gets a list of instances and picks one.

In discovery, the caller sends the request to a router/gateway. The router then queries the registry and forwards the call.

  • Client-side: one less network hop & callers can pick smarter routes.

  • But client-side needs a discovery library in every language you use.

  • Server-side: callers stay simple as the router does the lookup.

  • Yet the router adds an extra hop and must keep its address cache in sync.

“Which would you use on Kubernetes?”

Server-side, since it’s built in.

Each Service gets a stable DNS name, and the platform routes to healthy pods. A client-side library adds little there. If you need smarter routing, a service mesh adds it without code changes.

Mixing up the registry and discovery.

The registry stores where instances live… Discovery is how a caller uses it.

Treating them as one thing makes the answer vague.

“Order service needs customer details stored in customer database. How does it get them?”

Database per service means each service owns its data store, and other services reach data only through the owner’s API.

Order service owns the orders database. If shipping needs order details, it calls the order API or listens for order events. Each service can also pick the store that suits it best.

Search might use Elasticsearch while payments stays on PostgreSQL.

  • Never read another service’s tables directly!

  • Instead, call the customer API when you need fresh data.

  • Or keep a local read copy, updated from customer events for speed & resilience.

  • Tradeoff: API call is fresh but adds a runtime dependency, while a local copy is fast but slightly stale.

  • For reports across services, feed a separate read store from events.

“How do you make sure the event goes out whenever the data changes?”

Use the transactional outbox pattern:

Write the change and the event into the same local transaction, with the event in an outbox table. A separate relay reads the outbox and publishes each event.

This avoids a commit that succeeds while the publish fails.

Saying services could share one database as long as each uses its own tables. A shared database still schema changes, load, and outages across services.

“A customer places an order. You need to reserve stock, charge the card, and book delivery. Yet each step lives on a different service. How do you keep data correct?”

A saga splits one long transaction into a chain of local transactions, each with an undo step called a “compensating transaction".

An order saga might reserve stock, charge the card, and book delivery. Each step commits in its own service right away. If delivery booking fails, the saga runs compensations in reverse.

It refunds the card & releases the stock.

  • Explain why one database transaction cannot span three services.

  • Explain why two-phase commit is a poor fit: long locks across services hurt availability.

  • Walk through the saga: each step commits locally, each has a compensating step.

  • Name both styles of Saga. In “choreography”, services react to each other’s events. In “orchestration”, one orchestrator tells each service what to do next.

“What happens if the refund itself fails?”

Retry the compensation until it succeeds; every compensation must be idempotent. Plus, store the saga’s state, so a crash can resume from the last step.

If retries keep failing, raise an alert for manual handling.

Saying a saga keeps data consistent at every moment.

Other requests can see half-finished states between steps. Strong candidates say how they’d handle this, such as marking the order “pending” until the saga completes.

“Your order service calls a payment service. Payment starts timing out. What happens to the order service, and how do you protect it?”

A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing service once errors cross a threshold, then lets a few test calls through later.

The breaker starts closed and calls flow normally. When failures pass a set rate, it trips open. Every call now fails fast without touching the broken service. After a cooldown, it moves to half-open and allows a few test calls.

Success closes it again, but failure opens it again.

  • Threads in the order service wait on slow payment calls, pile up, and the order service fails as well.

  • A circuit breaker trips once the failure rate crosses a threshold, so calls fail fast.

  • Name the three states: closed, open, and half-open.

  • Pair the breaker with a timeout and a fallback. On its own, it only turns slow errors into fast ones.

“How do you pick the threshold?”

Start from real traffic data.

Use a failure rate over a sliding window, not a raw error count, so quiet periods don’t trip it. Set a minimum number of calls before it can trip. Then tune it from what you see in production.

Describing the breaker as a retry mechanism. Retries keep calling the broken service. A breaker stops calling it.

“You’re starting a new product with 5 engineers. Would you build a monolith or microservices?”

A monolith is one application where every module ships together as a single deployable unit.

Orders, payments, and user accounts live in one codebase. They share one process and usually one database. Modules talk through plain function calls, so each call is fast and fails loudly.

You build it once, test it once, and deploy it once.

  • Pick a monolith first. Five engineers ship faster with one codebase, one pipeline, and one deploy.

  • The product will change shape often, so service boundaries drawn now will probably be wrong.

  • Keep clean module boundaries inside the monolith. Each module owns its own tables, and other modules call it through a clear interface.

  • Name the signals for splitting later: builds get slow, engineers block each other’s releases, or one module needs to scale on its own.

“Your monolith has grown to 60 engineers. What do you do?”

Find the module with the most pain first, such as the one that changes most often or needs to scale most.

Extract it into its own service behind the same interface. Route traffic to the new service bit by bit, and keep the old code path until the new one proves stable.

Repeat one module at a time, never all at once.

Calling the monolith outdated by default.

Interviewers want to hear you match the architecture to the size of the group and the product. A rewrite into many services on day one is the answer they’re testing you against.

Shopify still runs a very large Rails monolith, so “monoliths don’t scale” sounds like you’re simply following trends.

8. Sidecar and service mesh

“When would you add a service mesh & what does it cost you?”

A service mesh is a layer of proxies, one beside each service, which handles all traffic between services.

Each proxy, called a sidecar, runs in the same pod as its service. Every request in and out passes through it. The sidecar handles encryption, retries, timeouts, and metrics. A control plane pushes rules to every sidecar at once.

You change a retry policy in one place, and the entire fleet follows.

  • It gives you encryption, retries, timeouts, and traffic metrics without code changes.

  • A service mesh becomes more useful when you have many microservices built with different programming languages.

  • But it adds extra delay on every call, extra memory in every pod, and makes the system complex.

  • Plus, debugging gets harder because a failure could occur in the proxy…not the service.

“How is a service mesh different from an API gateway?”

A gateway handles traffic coming into the system from clients…A mesh handles traffic between services inside the system.

Many large systems run both.

Adding a mesh to five services because it’s popular.

At that size, a library like Resilience4j covers retries and timeouts. Interviewers want to hear you weigh the running costs.

“Checkout request is slow & it touches ten services. How do you find the cause?”

Observability is your ability to understand a system’s inner state from logs, metrics, and traces it produces.

Logs record single events, like an error with its details. Metrics track numbers over time, like request rate and error rate. Traces follow one request across every service it touches.

Each service passes a shared trace ID along with the call. Your tracing tool then stitches the pieces into one timeline.

  • Start with a distributed trace. It shows how much time each service spent on the request.

  • Use metrics to spot which service’s latency or error rate went up.

  • Search the logs by trace ID to see the exact error.

  • Alert on what users feel, such as slow checkouts, not on every server metric.

“Tracing every request costs too much. What do you do?”

Sample. Keep a small share of normal traces and keep every trace with an error or a slow response. Set retention limits on logs as well.

Answering “I’d check the logs.”

Logs from ten services can’t be joined without a shared trace ID. Name tracing first.

10. Service-oriented architecture

“How is service-oriented architecture different from microservices?”

Service-oriented architecture () builds an application from large, shared services connected through a central messaging layer.

In SOA, one service covers an entire business function, like billing. Several applications reuse the same service. An enterprise service bus () sits in the middle. It routes messages, converts formats, and applies rules between services.

  • Size: SOA services are large and shared across applications. Microservices are small and built around one capability.

  • Logic: SOA puts routing and rules in the bus. Microservices keep the pipes simple and put logic inside each service.

  • Data: SOA services share a database. Each microservice owns its own data.

  • Releases: Shared SOA service needs sign-off from every consumer. A microservice ships on its own.

“Isn’t an API gateway just an enterprise service bus again?”

Only if you let it grow into one.

A gateway should route, check tokens, and apply rate limits. Once it starts holding business rules or joining data from many services, it becomes the bottleneck the bus was.

Watch for gateway changes in every feature release.

Saying “microservices are just SOA done right” without naming a single difference. Interviewers want concrete points. The bus and data ownership are the two clearest ones.

“How would you split an online shop’s monolith into services?”

A is a boundary inside which one domain model and its terms have one exact meaning.

Take the word “customer.” Sales sees a customer as a lead with a deal value. Support sees someone with open tickets. Shipping only needs a name and an address.

A bounded context lets each area keep its own small model instead of sharing one giant one.

  • Start from the business domain, not from database tables or code layers.

  • Find boundaries where words change meaning, such as “customer” or “product.”

  • Each context owns its model & data, and becomes a candidate service.

  • Map how contexts depend on each other, and which events pass between them.

  • Start with a few large contexts, and split further only when you have a reason.

“Two contexts both need customer data. Where does it live?”

One context owns the source of truth, such as customer service. It publishes an event whenever a customer changes. Other contexts keep their own copy with only the fields they need, updated from those events.

Splitting by technical layer, with one service for the user interface, one for logic, and one for data. Every feature then touches all three, so nothing ships alone. One service per database table fails the same way.

“Design rate limiting for a public API running on ten gateway instances.”

Rate limiting caps the number of requests a caller make in a set time window.

The gateway counts requests per user, API key, or IP address. Once a caller passes the limit, extra requests get an response. A common method is the token bucket.

Each caller has a bucket that refills at a steady rate & each request spends one token.

  • Limit per user or API key, not just per IP address.

  • Pick an algorithm: token bucket allows short bursts; sliding window gives smoother limits.

  • Also keep counters in a shared store like Redis, so all ten instances see the same count.

  • Return a with a header on limit.

  • Plus, set different limits per plan and per endpoint.

“Redis goes down. Do you block all traffic or let it through?”

Usually let it through, using rough limits inside each gateway instance.

An outage in the limiter then doesn’t become an outage of the entire API. For sensitive endpoints like login, block instead.

Counting inside each instance only. With ten instances, the real limit becomes ten times higher. Fixed time windows have a similar flaw since a caller can send double the limit on a window edge.

“Design a REST API for orders.”

Representational state transfer () is an API style where clients act on resources using standard HTTP methods.

A uniform resource locator () like names one order. GET reads it, POST creates one, PUT replaces it, and DELETE removes it. Responses normally come back as JSON.

Each request carries everything the server needs, so servers keep no session state between calls.

  • Use nouns for resources, such as and .

  • Use the right methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.

  • Return clear status codes, such as for created, for not found, and for a conflict.

  • Paginate lists, and plan how you’ll version the API.

“A client retries POST after a timeout. How do you avoid creating two orders?”

Ask the client to send an idempotency key with each POST. The server stores the key with the result. A repeat request with the same key returns the stored result instead of creating a new order.

Putting verbs in URLs, like , or returning for every error with the real problem hidden in the body.

What happens next is up to you. Because the next time an interviewer asks you to design a microservices system, the answer won’t come from this letter. It’ll come from what you’ve learned and practiced.

items.title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
items.author: sammatilda
items.content:
Feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I said to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”

Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely.

I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with.

Feynman was also quoted as saying:

I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.

Pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read:

What I cannot create, I do not understand.

items.title: Restricting AI agents in mobile operating systems platforms from capturing data
items.author: dotcoma
items.content:
Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.

People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.

We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.

We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:

  1. Developers should have an easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing, including (but not limited to) screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, all without undermining the core utility of an application.
  2. Operating system companies should create better documentation and technical specifications around how these AI agents function, particularly regarding data access and processing. Confidential computing approaches are not a complete solution, and do not address these core concerns. In particular, these approaches still leave the power to determine the extent of privacy guarantees (if any) in the hands of these providers.

We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

In addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry.

Finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes. We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.

items.title: Carnival Cruises emits ten times more sulphur oxide than all of Europe's cars (2019)
items.author: sammatilda
items.content:
In April, Ecohustler disrupted Carnival Cruise's AGM calling on the shareholders to reduce their company's pollution using straight forward and affordable methods - like burning cleaner fuel. Since then, a new report outlines the corporation's impact on the coastline of Europe. These vast floating cities are burning dirty bunker fuel and creating shocking levels of air pollution wherever they go. Shipping has been an unregulated industry for too long and action is urgently required.

Carnival Corporation, the world’s largest luxury cruise operator, emitted nearly 10 times more sulphur oxide (SOx) around European coasts than did all 260 million European cars in 2017, a new analysis by sustainable transport group Transport & Environment reveals.

Royal Caribbean Cruises, the world’s second largest, is second, yet four times worse than the European car fleet. SOx emissions form sulphate (SO4) aerosols that increase human health risks and contribute to acidification in terrestrial and aquatic environments.

SUPPORTED BY

JOIN US →

In absolute terms, Spain, Italy and Greece, closely followed by France and Norway, are the European countries most exposed to SOx air pollution from cruise vessels while Barcelona, Palma de Mallorca and Venice are the most impacted European port cities, followed by Civitavecchia (Rome) and Southampton.

All photos by Greg English ©

These countries are so exposed because they are major tourist destinations, but also because they have less stringent marine sulphur fuel standards which allows cruise ships to burn the dirtiest most sulphurous fuel all along their coastlines.

Faig Abbasov, shipping policy manager at T&E, said: “Luxury cruise ships are floating cities powered by some of the dirtiest fuel possible. Cities are rightly banning dirty diesel cars but they’re giving a free pass to cruise companies that spew out toxic fumes that do immeasurable harm both to those on board and on nearby shores. This is unacceptable.“

NOX emissions from cruise ships in Europe also heavily impact some cities, equivalent to about 15% of the nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted by Europe’s passenger car fleet in a year, the report finds. In Marseille, for example, 57 cruise ships emitted in 2017 almost as much NOx as one-quarter of the city’s 340,000 passenger cars. Along the coasts of countries such as Norway, Denmark, Greece, Croatia and Malta a handful of cruise ships are also responsible for more NOx than the majority of their domestic car fleet.

Europe should implement a zero-emission port standard as soon as possible, this could then be extended to other ship types. The report also recommends extending emission control areas (ECAs), currently in place only in the North and Baltic Seas and English Channel, to the rest of the European seas. Furthermore, the report recommends regulating NOx emissions from existing ships, which are currently exempt from NOx standards applying in emission control areas.

Faig Abbasov concluded “There are enough mature technologies to clean up cruise ships. Shore-side electricity can help cut in-port emissions, batteries are a solution for shorter distances and hydrogen technology can power even the biggest cruise ships. The cruise sector are apparently not willing to make the shift voluntarily, so we need governments to step in and mandate zero emission standards.”

    This previously returned .

  • Remove server variable (Thomas Munro) §

  • Change to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) §

    Previously was enabled by default, and activated based on optimizer costs, but this costing has been determined to be unreliable. This change requires sites that are doing many large analytical queries to manually enable .

  • Change parallel vacuum leaders and workers to share the cost-based vacuum delay limit (Bharath Rupireddy) §

    Previously each worker process slept based only on the cost it incurred itself, so a parallel vacuum could consume several times the budget set by . With this change, with parallel workers and cost-based delay enabled might run slower than in previous releases.

  • This is necessary since sequence errors are now tracked separately.

In databases with a locale provider other than libc (e.g., , ) and where the locale configured through that locale provider behaves differently from the setting configured for the database, particularly a LC_CTYPE of , the output of some full text search and functions could change. When upgrading such databases using , it is recommended to reindex all indexes which use full text search and after the upgrade, and to recompute any stored values.

items.title: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities across its supported versions, just four weeks after patches for the widely exploited PHP2Shell flaws. SecurityWeek reports: One of the security defects expected to be resolved is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution (RCE) defect in the file-upload progress tracking functionality. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed two days after PHP2Shell made headlines. PHP's maintainers warned at the time that the security flaw can be triggered only under an unusual combination of configuration and code.
 
"An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled," PHP said last month. Noting that patches would be released as part of the regular update cycle, PHP developers recommended disabling session upload, a setting also listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two RCE bugs tracked as PHP2Shell.

items.title: Google Will Launch Android App Verification Requirement Globally In January 2027
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven't registered their apps to do so soon.
 
The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google's new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won't be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure. Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.
 
In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it's not wasting any time with the January start. It says that verification will reach all devices within "several months." So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with "millions" of non-Play apps already registered. The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

items.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
items.author: cybermango
items.content:
Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here.

Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.

One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.

The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.

In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question, but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.

The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called .

Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested.

Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction.

Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together.

In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them.

A note about Claude’s methods

In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks.

The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other.

The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model. Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result.

The Hawking-Page transition

To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City.

Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously.

This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave.

To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its . Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics.

This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out.

Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from.

Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the , which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature.

At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition.

It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins.

This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information.

In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality.

In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision.) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing?

For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as . This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there.

Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual.

When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps . In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed.

The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result.

To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature.

The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between.

This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all.

Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.)

Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future.

As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim.

As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality.

Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one.

Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model, a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems.

In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the , which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own.

Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies.

To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension.

The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or . There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time.

In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment.

Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer.

If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out.

The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories?

This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics.

The goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin.

Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question.

Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a . Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper.

This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search.

These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research.

items.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
items.author: cybermango
items.content:
A virus has stopped pancreatic cancer in its tracks in three people in a clinical trial in the US. Further evaluation is needed in larger trials, but the early results are encouraging, especially since only small doses of the virus were administered for initial safety testing.

“We only injected one-tenth of the dose we are eventually aiming at, so the efficacy is better than I expected, especially as this is pancreatic cancer,” says Masato Yamamoto at the University of Minnesota, who led the development of the viral treatment.

Pancreatic cancer is notorious for being the deadliest type of the condition. One reason is that symptoms tend to appear late, when the cancer has already spread and cannot be surgically removed. Once diagnosed, people usually live only around three to six months.

Another reason is that pancreatic tumours have tough, fibrous exteriors that block chemotherapy drugs from getting in. “They’re hard as hockey pucks,” says Yamamoto. Immunotherapies that boost immune activity against cancer are also ineffective, because pancreatic tumours can hide from the immune system.

The first patient in the trial, who had a pancreatic tumour 7 centimetres across, was administered the treatment a year ago, and the other two have been since then. At the time, their tumours hadn’t spread beyond the pancreas. Since being treated, their tumours haven’t grown any further. “They are all still alive and have clinically stable disease,” says Yamamoto, who presented the results at the annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy in Boston, Massachusetts, earlier this month. Another 15 patients will now be given higher doses to find the optimum level.

“I think this is an interesting early signal, but as a pancreatic surgeon, I think it’s important to keep perspective,” says Kai Brown at Royal North Shore Hospital in Sydney. “The history of oncology is littered with promising early signals that vanished by the time rigorous phase III [late-stage] testing was done, so I think these preliminary conference results should probably just be seen as hypothesis-generating at this stage.” He also notes that the trial so far hasn’t included a control group, so it is hard to know whether the cancer-killing virus works better than other treatments or none at all.

The virus is an adenovirus that has been genetically engineered to replicate only inside tumours and not healthy tissue. Its replication is specifically activated by an enzyme called cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), which is present at much higher levels in cancer cells than in normal ones. After cancer cells become infected with the virus, they burst open and die, releasing more virus that can infect neighbouring cancer cells.

In the trial, the virus was injected directly into the patients’ tumours through a thin tube that was guided down a patient’s throat to their pancreas. The tube had an ultrasound probe on the end to allow visualisation of the tumours.

The reason the tumours have stopped growing but haven’t become any smaller may be due to the low treatment dose, says Yamamoto. He thinks they may start to shrink as the virus has more time to replicate.

As the tumour cells start to break apart and leak their contents, the immune system may also be able to recognise and fight the cancer, says Yamamoto. “The patient’s immune system can realise something is wrong, and then go and attack the tumour,” he says. The hope is that the immune system will also recognise and destroy any tumour cells that have spread to other parts of the body. If so, the treatment could be effective against metastatic pancreatic cancer.

To try to supercharge this natural immune response, Yamamoto and his colleagues are now planning to combine the viral treatment with immunotherapies like checkpoint inhibitors – drugs that block proteins that stop the immune system from attacking the cancer cells – in future clinical trials.

Adenoviruses, which cause cold- and flu-like symptoms in their unmodified forms, have a long history of being investigated as potential cancer treatments. In the 1950s, for instance, women with cervical cancer were injected with an unmodified adenovirus in a clinical trial, with partial success. However, it became clear that adenoviruses must be engineered to make them selectively target cancer cells, for safety and efficacy reasons.

The only cancer-killing virus that has been approved by the Food and Drug Administration in the US is T-VEC, a genetically modified herpes simplex virus that is injected directly into melanoma tumours, causing the cells to rupture and die.
