Oh, and oh so give us your fucking ID or passport! We won’t leak it later, promise!

And you may just get fucked anyway and not get approval. Approval to appropriately protect your own service!

This wasn’t the first time I ran into this issue. As maddening as it sounds, I to keep up with the security landscape and to apply appropriate mitigations because leaking sensitive information is and I can’t let that happen.

If there’s a popular exploit out there that applies for our technical stack, I need to know if the public proof-of-concept snippets can be adapted and used maliciously against my services. But no, Claude will tell you to fuck off and use an older model that will try to stop you from applying adequate protection.

You know who don’t need to ask for approval? Criminals. They just go and use the models that don’t have safeguards in place. Abliterated open weights models don’t care. Bad actors reach their goals with or without your “safe” models.

You can use a knife to cut up some food, or seriously hurt someone. Yet I don’t get asked to put in an application with my government-provided ID to buy one. Why is this tool so special?

Predictably, the only way to make our own service more secure ended up involving the use of EU-hosted open weights models, such as GLM 5.3, that actually complied with our intentions, proved that the issue is there, and then helped fix and verify that the issue is now resolved, for good.

Congratulations, Anthropic, you’ve made the world an unsafer place.

Or maybe that was your plan all along to get regulators to react and build that moat for you right before your IPO to fend off competitors?

Either way, I’m just incredibly frustrated. Big AI labs use the same tools without restrictions to make the security landscape a fucking mess, and then they go and prohibit others from using the same tools to protect themselves from the threats they just created. Fucking asshats.

items.title: How GraphRAG Works - A Deep Dive
items.author: Neo Kim
items.content:
Most SaaS products start with Admin, Editor, and Viewer.

Then a 30,000-person enterprise signs up with matrix reporting, regional compliance, and its own idea of who sees what. Custom roles pile up per tenant, and deals stall on access rules your model can’t express.50+ page guide by Cerbos co-founder Emre Baran shows how to implement authorization that fits each tenant without adding roles for every customer.

  • at enterprise scale, and what role explosion looks like

  • Letting customers manage their own roles with delegated admin

  • Keeping each tenant’s policies platform-wide rules and out of your application code

  • Real examples from leading SaaS companies scaling authorization across thousands of tenants

Useful if you’re building multitenant SaaS or about to sign one of your first large enterprise customers.

(Thanks to Cerbos for partnering on this newsletter.)

Picture yourself starting a new software project.

You search the codebase for a function, class, and/or configuration file. But finding those pieces is only the job…

You need to understand how they connect:

Which service calls this function?

Which database it depend on?

Which business rule affects the result?

AI systems face a similar problem.

Traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation () retrieves relevant chunks from a large document collection. But what happens when many documents contain parts of the answer, and the true answer depends on their relationships?

That is where GraphRAG takes a unique approach:

It connects information instead of seeing it as separate pieces. It links entities, concepts, people, events & documents into a knowledge graph. Now the system searches for relevant information and follows connections between them.

Here’s what you'll find in this newsletter:

  • Why finding the right text isn’t always enough: where traditional RAG and vector search fall short when an answer depends on relationships between people, documents, concepts, and events.

  • How GraphRAG connects the dots. How knowledge graphs turn scattered information into connected knowledge, and how GraphRAG uses those connections to retrieve better answers.

  • How GraphRAG finds the right path: From graph queries and traversal to local, global, multi-hop, path, and community-based retrieval. Learn why different questions need different paths.

  • How you know GraphRAG actually works. How to assess retrieval for relevance, faithfulness, completeness, speed, and overall quality, and what happens when the graph grows very large.

  • What happens when RAG starts making decisions. How Agentic RAG moves beyond a fixed retrieval pipeline by choosing retrieval strategies, tools, and sources based on the question.

RAG is a key method for enterprise apps.

It gives Large Language Models () access to information outside their training data. It gathers relevant content from sources such as company documents, knowledge bases & databases. Then it forwards that information to the LLM to generate a response.

Let’s break down what RAG is:

  • Locate information from an outside source

  • Add information that was retrieved to the model context

  • Generate an answer based on provided context using LLM

Think of RAG as an information desk for an LLM.

The retrieval system finds the information and gives it to the LLM so it can answer the question.

Let’s look at the standard RAG pipeline (step by step)…

There are 2 phases in a RAG system:

  1. Indexing stage (onetime/periodic)

  2. Query stage (for queries from the user)

Let’s walk through key steps in a RAG pipeline:

Get the documents you want the system to use as references.

  • Legal documents, precedents, agreements & decisions

  • Literature & clinical guidelines

  • Documentation, code repositories, or API documentation

  • Customer support tickets & FAQ databases

Extract useful, machine-readable content from raw sources.

This includes PDFs, documents, web pages, and databases. It uses PDF parsers, web crawlers, and optical character recognition () tools.

Chunk the documents.

Even the latest LLM models have a small context window (even 1M tokens don’t mean you can feed your entire knowledge base into each prompt!). So break documents into tiny pieces, typically 200-1000 tokens long.

Split text into fixed-size chunks, semantic chunks, or recursive chunks.

  • divides text into equal-length pieces.

  • gathers related content.

  • breaks text into smaller parts step by step.

These chunks enter an embedding model.

The neural network turns each chunk into a dense numerical vector with 768 to 1,536 elements. These vectors depict . The system will cluster similar-looking chunks together, even when they use different words.

Here are the popular embedding models:

  • Voyage AI’s voyage-large-2

  • OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-large

  • Open-source solutions such as BGE, E5 & GTE

A vector database stores these embeddings & enables fast similarity searches.

Let’s see how to find information relevant to a user’s query…

When a user asks a question, the system creates an embedding.

This guarantees the query vector is in the same semantic space as the document vectors.

The system then sends the query embedding to the vector database.

The database checks the query vector against the stored document vectors. It then identifies the most semantically similar chunks.

The vector database runs k-nearest neighbors () search to identify the K document chunks closest to the query embedding.

Here are the typical measures of similarity:

  • Measures the angle between two vectors. The closer their directions, the more similar their embeddings.

  • Fast to compute, appropriate for normalized vectors.

  • Measures straight-line distance.

Yet exact k-NN search is too expensive at scale.

Vector databases enable billion-scale searches in milliseconds using approximate nearest neighbor () methods. These include Hierarchical Navigable Small World () graphs & Inverted File Index ().

Prompt construction.

The prompt includes the retrieved chunks inserted in the following format:

You are a helpful assistant.

Answer the user’s question using only the information
provided in the context below.

The system provides the LLM with the prompt and extra context.

Then, the LLM creates a response based on the information it has retrieved. A successful RAG implementation must have the model reference its sources.

This enables verification & builds trust.

Thus, LLM answers questions it has NOT encountered before, such as your company’s internal documents, research papers, customer tickets, and so on.

RAG would find the right pieces of information but miss the relationships between them. And when the answer depends on those connections, simply finding relevant chunks is NOT enough.

Problems with Standard RAG

As data size grows, vector search becomes less accurate. (The accuracy could drop by 12% when the collection grows from 10,000 to 100,000 pages.)

The more documents you add, the more the embeddings overlap, and the more difficult the system will find it to locate the right chunks.

But scaling is not the entire story…

Standard RAG has two fundamental limitations, and they become HARD to ignore as the system grows:

1. Chunks are treated as separate

Once the system chunks & embeds a document, it converts the document into individual, independent vectors.

With RAG, there is no explicit link between chunks (even within the same/different documents). Vector search finds relevant chunks based on vector similarity.

This makes it harder to connect related facts across documents.

2. RAG cannot reason across documents

Some questions require information from many documents/sources.

RAG retrieves information chunks relevant to the question. Yet it does not link these chunks to show their relationships. This makes it hard to ask questions about the entire document collection.

These limitations make it harder for standard RAG to connect related information across chunks & documents…This is where takes retrieval a step further!

GraphRAG adds structure to your documents and does NOT treat them as disjointed chunks in vector space.

An LLM processes each piece of text, identifies entities, and the relationships between them. These entities become nodes in a knowledge graph, and the relationships become edges connecting these nodes.

So you end up with a neat graph of your entire dataset, showing how your data is related in reality across documents.

GraphRAG does more than match text to your query:

It infers facts from related entities. Plus, it traces facts across documents & find information spread across various texts. And answers questions about the entire dataset.

Let’s follow the journey from raw documents to a searchable knowledge graph…

  1. Indexing Stage (constructing knowledge graph)

  2. Query Stage (retrieving from the knowledge graph)

The general pipeline has two extra steps:

  • Community detection: groups related entities into clusters. For example, people, companies, and products that frequently connect.

  • Community summarization: An LLM creates a short report with the important information inside each community.

Think of it like organizing a huge library…

Instead of reading every book whenever someone asks a broad question, you first group related books into sections and create a summary for each section.

At query time, GraphRAG uses these summaries to answer big-picture questions about the dataset without examining every entity & relationship individually.

GraphRAG vs Microsoft GraphRAG

GraphRAG is a general approach to RAG.

Instead of relying only on similar text chunks, it uses a Knowledge Graph to connect related entities & information.

Microsoft GraphRAG is a specific implementation of this idea…Its pipeline includes:

  • Entity & relationship extraction

  • Different retrieval methods--Local Search & Global Search

Think of GraphRAG as the idea of making pizza and Microsoft GraphRAG as one specific pizza recipe.

The idea tells you what you are trying to build… The recipe gives you specific steps for how to build it.

Next, let’s look at Knowledge Graphs & how they “connect” information…

Let’s start with the basic building blocks:

Nodes, Edges, and Properties

A Knowledge Graph shows how different pieces of information connect:

  • Things in the graph, such as a person, company, product, or place

  • Relationships connecting those things

  • Extra information about nodes/relationships

A “basic graph” tells you what connects to what…While a “property graph” tells you what those things are & what the connection means.

Think of a knowledge graph as a map of knowledge and a property graph as a way of putting extra details on that map.

Let’s understand it with an example:

= Connected FactsJohn Le Carré → WROTE → Book

= Connected Facts With Extra Details

John Le Carré → WROTE → Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy ← PURCHASED (03-02-2011) ← Ian

Resource Description Framework () is a standard way to represent & link information on the Web using triples.

A triplet is a basic unit of data in the graph.

And each triple contains three parts:

Subject → Predicate → Object

  1. Node associated with the triplet

  2. Node receiving the relationship points

  3. Relationship between subject & object

  • John le Carre, Graham Greene, Ian, Alan

  • Wrote, Purchased

  • Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy

RDF lets users merge data from various sources without losing original details.

i.e., you query the complete global dataset instead of specific data instances. RDFs let knowledge graphs carry properties from different data management models.

  • Organize data from many sources into a unified collection for querying & searching.

  • Allow analysis of a networked structure.

  • Store information collected from different sources to answer questions or support decisions.

RDF Schema and Ontologies

RDF Schema () is a technique to describe classes & relationships with RDF data.

For example, you can define a person & book as classes and define relationships between them.

An ontology goes beyond a dictionary… It formally defines concepts in a domain and shows how they relate to one another.

A health domain ontology could define:

Researcher ──conducts→ Clinical trial

Clinical Trial ──studies→ Disease

Clinical Trial ──tests→ Drug

The ontology gives the graph meaning & a common vocabulary.

Cypher & SPARQL (SPARQL Protocol & RDF Query Language) are 2 graph query languages.

is a query language used with property graphs.

It has syntax that directly specifies graph patterns:

MATCH (p:Person {name: "John le Carré"})-[:WROTE]->(b:Book)

This query finds the person named John Le Carré.

It follows WROTE relationship to locate the connected book & return the book’s title.

is a query language for RDF.

It operates on RDF triples rather than on property graph patterns:

PREFIX : <http://example.org/>

SELECT ?book
WHERE {
  :JohnLeCarre :wrote ?book .
}

These languages retrieve related information, but they use different graph models.

This is key for GraphRAG retrieval… Queries fetch data from relationships, not just similar meanings.

Vector Database and Knowledge Graph

Vector databases find information based on .

A knowledge graph is a collection of entities & their relationships. You link entities & explore how they relate to each other.

i.e., vector search finds relevant information…while knowledge graphs link the dots.

Who has written research papers on Alzheimer’s disease?

This involves multiple relationships:

Researcher → Published → Paper → Studies → Disease → Treatment

Also they could work together:

  • Vector search finds relevant papers, but it doesn't represent specific relationships in the vector space.

  • A knowledge graph directly stores these relationships, thus making it easier to track multi-step questions.

How to Choose Between Graph and Vector Databases

Before choosing a database, answer these questions:

  • What types of data will you store: documents, embeddings, entities, or relationships?

  • Do queries rely primarily on semantic similarity or explicit relationships?

  • Do you need multi-hop traversal across connected entities?

  • Do you need to represent multiple relationship types & properties?

  • Do queries combine semantic retrieval with graph traversal?

  • What are your latency, throughput & scalability requirements?

  • How frequently will your data & relationships change?

  • Which query languages, APIs, and ecosystem integrations do you need?

  • Use vector search for semantic similarity

  • Use graph databases for relationship-heavy queries, and hybrid retrieval when you need both.

Ontology and Schema Design

Before building a Knowledge Graph, decide which entities, relationships, and properties it should contain.

A schema defines the structure of your graph, while an ontology describes the meaning of its concepts and relationships.

For example, in a medical research knowledge graph:

  • Researcher, Paper, Disease, Treatment

  • AUTHORED, STUDIES, TREATS

  • Name, publication date, research field

There are two popular approaches to schema design:

1. Top-Down Schema Design

Start with a domain model that defines the entities & relationships…Then build the graph according to that model.

Think of building a house. You create the blueprint first, then construct the house.

Similarly, you define the graph’s structure before adding data.

When you know the domain well and need consistent terminology and relationships.

2. Bottom-Up Schema Design

Start with the available data.

Identify important entities and relationships, then use them to develop the schema.

Imagine having a collection of building materials. You inspect what is available before deciding how to design the house.

When you have massive collections of unstructured documents and don’t know all the relationships in advance.

In practice, you can combine both approaches…

Start with a basic schema, extract entities and relationships from your documents, then refine the schema as you discover new patterns.

Common Schema Design Pitfalls

Without rules for growth, a knowledge graph becomes hard to manage.

Here are 5 common mistakes:

  • The same real-world entity appears as multiple nodes. For example, “John Smith” and “J. Smith” might refer to the same researcher but exist as separate nodes.

  • Important connections between entities are absent. For example, a Student and Course exist as nodes, but the ENROLLED_IN relationship between them is missing.

  • Too many entity types, relationships, and/or properties make the graph difficult to understand & query. For example, storing every student’s phone number, age, and email address as separate nodes when simple properties would be enough.

  • Inconsistent relationship names: Different names describe the same relationship. For example, AUTHORED, WROTE, and IS_AUTHOR_OF might represent the same connection between a researcher and a paper.

  • Schema designed for a single query: A graph built to answer one specific question might struggle with new questions. For example, a university graph designed only to find students enrolled in courses might lack the relationships needed to identify their instructors.

The goal is not to model every possible detail…

Instead, design a graph that captures the entities and relationships your application needs, while leaving room for new use cases.

Let’s see how GraphRAG uses this structure to retrieve information and generate answers…

GraphRAG combines knowledge graphs with RAG to find information, follow relationships & generate answers grounded in relevant evidence.

The pipeline has 3 key stages:

  1. Build & store the knowledge graph.

  2. Detect communities & generate summaries.

  3. Retrieve relevant information & generate an answer.

Step 1: Knowledge Graph Creation

Convert raw documents into a structured graph of entities & relationships.

Collect information from sources such as books, articles, research papers & internal documents.

For example, a medical research system processes thousands of papers about diseases, treatments, and clinical trials.

2. Entity and Relationship Extraction

Identify important entities & relationships between them.

You could use LLMs, Named Entity Recognition (), and/or rule-based methods.

“Dr. Smith authored a paper about a new treatment for Alzheimer’s disease.”

The extraction process identifies:

  • Dr. Smith, Research Paper, Treatment, Alzheimer’s Disease

  • AUTHORED, STUDIES, TREATS

Also, the system should resolve duplicate entities & validate extracted relationships before adding them to the graph.

Turn the extracted information into nodes, edges & properties:

  • Represent entities such as researchers, papers, diseases & treatments.

  • Connect related entities through relationships such as AUTHORED.

  • Store extra details such as names, publication dates, and research fields.

Dr. Smith → AUTHORED → Research Paper → STUDIES → Alzheimer's Disease

The result is a graph that captures both information & how different facts connect.

Store the graph in a graph database like Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, TigerGraph, or NebulaGraph.

Graph databases support relationship traversal & pattern matching.

You could query a graph to find all researchers who authored papers about treatments for a specific disease.

Neo4j is a common GraphRAG choice because it supports the Cypher query language, graph algorithms, and vector indexes.

Plus, you could combine a graph database with a specialized vector database such as Milvus, Pinecone, or Weaviate.

This gives your retrieval system access to semantic similarity & explicit relationships.

Step 2: Community Detection and Summaries

A large knowledge graph might contain millions of nodes & relationships.

And searching the entire graph for every question is going to be expensive.

Community detection organizes the graph into related groups…

A community is a group of nodes with relatively strong connections to one another.

Think of your social network:

You have friends, family members & coworkers. Each group forms a community because its members often share stronger connections with one another than with people outside the group.

Knowledge graphs work similarly…

A medical research graph might contain communities focused on cancer research, cardiovascular diseases, and neurological disorders.

Community-detection algorithms identify these groups based on the graph’s structure.

Here are the popular approaches:

  • Finds communities & refines their structure.

  • Groups nodes by optimizing modularity, a measure of community structure.

  • Groups nodes by repeatedly propagating labels across their connections.

Once the system identifies communities, an LLM summarizes each group.

A community about Alzheimer’s disease might include researchers, treatments, clinical trials & related papers. The LLM examines the available entity descriptions and relationships, then creates a report about the community.

These reports help GraphRAG answer broad questions without retrieving every individual node & relationship.

“What are the major research trends in Alzheimer’s treatment?”

Instead of examining thousands of disconnected facts at query time, system uses relevant community reports to identify important themes.

Step 3: Retrieval and Response Generation

Once the graph & community reports are ready, GraphRAG answers user questions.

The retrieval process has 4 parts:

System analyzes user’s question to identify relevant entities, relationships & search intent.

“Who are friends of my friends?”

In a social network graph, system starts from your user node & follows two friendship relationships.

You could express this with Cypher:

MATCH (:User {userId: 'referenceUser'})
      -[:FRIEND]->
      (:User)
      -[:FRIEND]->
      (fof:User)
RETURN DISTINCT fof

In a real app, you’d filter out original user & exclude existing direct friends.

The same principle applies to GraphRAG: start with relevant entities and follow meaningful relationships.

The system retrieves a relevant portion of the knowledge graph - .

  • Find entities & relationships directly relevant to question.

  • Follow additional relationships to gather supporting evidence.

“Which researchers are studying treatments for Alzheimer’s disease?”

Here’s what system would do:

  1. Find Alzheimer’s Disease node.

  2. Follow relationships to relevant treatments & research papers.

  3. Find the researchers who authored those papers.

  4. Retrieve supporting text from the original documents.

You control how far system explores using hop limits, relationship filters, and relevance scores.

This prevents retrieval from expanding into unrelated parts of the graph.

3. Information Aggregation

Combine retrieved entities, relationships & supporting text into context for LLM.

The system would collect:

  • Researchers & their publications

  • Treatments discussed in those publications

  • Relationships between treatments & diseases

  • Supporting passages from research papers

The goal is to give the LLM enough evidence to answer the question without overwhelming it with information.

LLM uses the retrieved context to generate a natural-language answer.

It identify researchers studying Alzheimer’s treatments and explain which papers support those connections.

When the system preserves source references, it also cite documents behind its answer. The key difference is GraphRAG retrieves information through both relevance & relationships.

  • Vector search helps find semantically similar content.

  • Graph traversal helps uncover how entities connect.

They provide a richer context for questions that depend on many connected facts.

Now we understand GraphRAG… when should we use it instead of standard RAG?

GraphRAG vs Standard RAG: when to use each

GraphRAG complements traditional vector RAG…Each approach serves different retrieval needs.

Consider using GraphRAG when:

  • Your documents contain relationships between entities, events, concepts.

  • Questions must draw connections between facts, follow a sequence, or look for patterns.

  • Answers require identifying themes, patterns, trends across an entire dataset.

  • You need to explore dependencies or trace connections between entities.

  • Your app benefits from structured, relationship-aware retrieval, such as legal research, scientific research, fraud investigation.

Consider using Vector RAG when:

  • Questions require straightforward factual lookups, such as “What is our annual leave policy?”

  • Relevant information is available in one or a few retrieved chunks.

  • Semantic similarity is sufficient to find the required information.

  • You want a simple retrieval architecture with lower indexing & maintenance overhead.

When you upgrade, you’ll get:

  • High-level architecture of real-world systems.

  • Deep dive into how popular real-world systems work.

  • How real-world systems handle scale, reliability & performance.

items.title: How the European Commission rolled out Matrix to more than 40k staff
items.author: liotier
items.content:
The European Commission went from a Matrix proof of concept in December 2025 to a sovereign communication tool rolled out to every Commission laptop by September 2026. That tool, built on Matrix by Element, and run by the Commission itself, now serves more than 40,000 users.

At The Matrix Conference 2026, Diana Gheorghe, Head of Sector for Digital Workplace Communication and Collaboration Services, and Alexandru Vignide, Service Delivery Manager for the Commission's sovereign communication tool, told the story of how they got there. The pair were transparent about what got harder at scale, and how they dealt with it.

Sovereignty means more than where the servers sit

“Sovereignty” can have a different meaning for different people and organisations, so the Commission started by pinning down what it means for them. Their answer spans five dimensions: resilience and business continuity, vendor diversity, control over their data, ownership of the platform, and leverage in procurement - the ability to negotiate with, or walk away from, a supplier. That last one is easy to forget, and arguably the one that bites hardest when it's missing.

For internal communications specifically, the priorities were resilience, data ownership and, crucially, interoperability. That's what led them to Matrix: an open protocol whose value lies in letting separate systems talk to each other. They chose Element Server Suite Pro (ESS Pro), Element's enterprise distribution of Matrix, as a mature implementation, and decided to host, operate and architect the service under their own control.

Sovereign cloud hosting, familiar login, without federation (yet)

With the building blocks chosen, Alexandru walked through three architecture decisions.

The service doesn't run in a Commission-owned data centre. Instead it runs with sovereign cloud providers selected through the sovereign hosting tender awarded earlier this year, in order to meet its sovereignty and hosting requirements. Sovereign doesn't have to mean building everything in-house; it means choosing who you depend on, and on what terms.

The deployment is integrated with EU Login, the sign-in staff already use every day. A new tool is easier to adopt when logging in feels familiar.

Connecting to Matrix servers outside the Commission is still under assessment. The technical side is being explored - there was a separate hands-on demo using non-production environments at the conference - but federation also needs governance, participation and structure, which takes longer to agree than a config change.

The Commission started working with Matrix in summer 2025, or, as Alexandru put it, at last year's Matrix Conference. From there, things moved quickly:

  1. the architecture and engineering team delivered a proof of concept showing Matrix and Element were viable for the Commission. It earned a green light for a Commission-wide service, which Alexandru described as a nice Christmas present.
  2. the team built the production infrastructure, along with the hosting and operations needed to run it, and was ready by June.
  3. a laptop pilot covering both the desktop and web clients, followed by a mobile pilot through the Commission's mobile device management (MDM) platform.
  4. the laptop rollout to all Commission users, delivered in waves, was and completed in September.

The Commission is now exploring a mobile rollout, and what federation could look like.

Scaling to 40,000 users brought challenges

Rolling out to 40,000 people surfaces problems no pilot will. Alexandru described the four main ones his team ran into, and how they tackled each.

Finding colleagues across servers. The Commission runs several Synapse homeservers, and early on, people on different servers couldn't always find each other. The Commission's teams worked with Element to fix this, and now a plain user search finds anyone in the Commission, whichever server they're on.

Accounts that only appear after sign-up. The Commission chose user-led account creation rather than pre-provisioning every account. The catch is that you can't find a colleague who hasn't registered yet, which made the discovery problem above feel worse while adoption was still ramping up.

Live presence was switched off. As more users came on board, the load from live presence (the real-time “online/away” indicator) started to affect performance, so the team disabled it. They're now looking at a user status feature being developed with Element as the replacement.

Infrastructure had to learn to scale itself. Rolling out in waves over three months meant uneven, shifting demand, so the team tuned the infrastructure to adjust automatically.

Running through all of this was the balance between security and usability. Most of the hardening work was done with the Commission's security teams before the rollout, and continues through regular security reviews and continuous improvements. The team made sure that hardening didn't get in the way of everyday tasks like creating an account, recovering it or verifying a new device, and documented those steps clearly for staff. Feedback from tickets, internal forums and public channels is consolidated into prioritised goals for the Commission's own roadmap.

The most common question, Diana said, is whether Element is meant to replace Microsoft Teams, or consumer apps like Signal and WhatsApp. The short answer: neither, directly. Element is positioned as an internal communication tool for specific use cases - secure communication among them - where the Commission's existing stack doesn't fully meet its needs. Teams bundles communication, collaboration and a whole platform behind it, so there's no one-to-one swap to be had.

That makes expectation-setting part of the job. People naturally compare workplace tools with the apps they use at home and go looking for feature-for-feature matches. Diana's view is that this mindset is something to address head-on in any organisational change: Element is a tool in its own right, with its own feature set, that the Commission and Element can evolve together.

Part of the goal is to bring work conversations onto a tool the Commission controls. 

Federation goes beyond tech

The Commission has been interested in federation for a long time. The obvious starting point is other EU institutions, but it wouldn't stop there: the Commission also works closely with member states, governments and non-governmental organisations.

No decision has been made yet, and the Commission is taking it one step at a time. First comes the technical question of what the technology can actually do, because, as Diana put it, there's no point writing policies technology can't deliver. Then comes governance: who the partners would be, on what terms, with what scope, and how security and privacy are handled.

Alexandru ended the talk by sharing what the deployment had taught the Commission.

Sovereignty is operational. It depends on operational control and the trustworthiness of the whole chain of partners, not just on where the service is hosted.

Adoption depends on everyday usability. Discoverability, onboarding support and everything around the product shape whether people use it.

Interoperability needs more than technology. It also needs clear structure, participation and governance.

He also noted that introducing a new communication tool has been a journey, and still is. Along the way, the Commission has relied on trustworthy service providers, and he described the collaboration with Element as a success.

items.title: Do not buy RAM, compress
items.author: Ecno92
items.content:
AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations. Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option. Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in , a solution to compress memory.

Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it. Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM. Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default. Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines. Most other distributions do not have it enabled.

Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes. What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4.

I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app. Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression. This could have cut our Cloud spend in half!

I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. (I have 32GB with some reserved for the graphics)
